problem.paragraph: A particle moving in a planar force field has a position vector $$\textbf{x}$$ that satisfies $$\mathbf{x}\prime = A\textbf{x}$$ . The $$2 \times 2$$ matrix $$A$$ has eigenvalues $$4$$ and $$2$$ , with corresponding eigenvectors $$\textbf{v}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 3} \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 1} \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Find the position of the particle at time $$t$$ , assuming that $$\textbf{x}(0) = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 6} \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ .

Let $$A$$ be a $$2 \times 2$$ matrix with eigenvalues $$- 3$$ and $$- 1$$ and corresponding eigenvectors $$\textbf{v}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 1} \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Let $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ be the position of a particle at time $$t$$ . Solve the initial value problem $$\mathbf{x}\prime = A\textbf{x}$$ , $$\textbf{x}(0) = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ .

exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 3–6, solve the initial value problem $$\mathbf{x}\prime(t) = A\textbf{x}(t)$$ for $$t \geq 0$$ , with $$\textbf{x}(0) = (3,2)$$ . Classify the nature of the origin as an attractor, repeller, or saddle point of the dynamical system described by $$\mathbf{x}\prime = A\textbf{x}$$ . Find the directions of greatest attraction and/or repulsion. When the origin is a saddle point, sketch typical trajectories.

In Exercises 7 and 8, make a change of variable that decouples the equation $$\mathbf{x}\prime = A\textbf{x}$$ . Write the equation $$\textbf{x}(t) = P\textbf{y}(t)$$ and show the calculation that leads to the uncoupled system $$\mathbf{y}\prime = D\textbf{y}$$ , specifying $$P$$ and $$D$$ .

In Exercises 9–18, construct the general solution of $$\mathbf{x}\prime = A\textbf{x}$$ involving complex eigenfunctions and then obtain the general real solution. Describe the shapes of typical trajectories.

where $$i_{L}$$ is the current through the inductor $$L$$ and $$v_{C}$$ is the voltage drop across the capacitor $$C$$ . problem.paragraph: Yes, the $$3 \times 3$$ matrix is diagonalizable because it has three distinct eigenvalues. Theorem 2 in Section 5.1 and Theorem 6 in Section 5.3 are valid when complex scalars are used. (The proofs are essentially the same as for real scalars.)

The general solution has the form $$x ( t ) = c_{1} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ - 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} e^{- . 5 t} + c_{2} \begin{bmatrix} 1 + 2 i \\ 4 i \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} e^{\left(\right. . 2 + . 3 t \left.\right) t} + c_{3} \begin{bmatrix} 1 - 2 i \\ - 4 i \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} e^{\left(\right. . 2 - . 3 i \left.\right) t}$$

The scalars $$c_{1}$$ , $$c_{2}$$ , and $$c_{3}$$ here can be any complex numbers. The first term in $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ is real, provided $$c_{1}$$ is real. Two more real solutions can be produced using the real and imaginary parts of the second term in $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ : $$\begin{bmatrix} 1 + 2 i \\ 4 i \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} e^{. 2 t} ( cos . 3 t + i sin . 3 t )$$

The general real solution has the following form, with real scalars $$c_{1}$$ , $$c_{2}$$ , and $$c_{3}$$ : $$c_{1} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ - 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} e^{- 5 t} + c_{2} \begin{bmatrix} cos . 3 t - 2 sin . 3 t \\ - 4 sin . 3 t \\ 2 cos . 3 t \end{bmatrix} e^{. 2 t} + c_{3} \begin{bmatrix} sin . 3 t + 2 cos . 3 t \\ 4 cos . 3 t \\ 2 sin . 3 t \end{bmatrix} e^{. 2 t}$$

Any solution with $$c_{2} = c_{3} = 0$$ is attracted to the origin because of the negative exponential factor. Other solutions have components that grow without bound, and the trajectories spiral outward.

list.item: Be careful not to mistake this problem for one in Section 5.6. There the condition for attraction toward $$\textbf{0}$$ was that an eigenvalue be less than $$1$$ in magnitude, to make $$| \text{λ} |^{k}\rightarrow 0$$ . Here the real part of the eigenvalue must be negative, to make $$e^{ \text{λ} t}\rightarrow 0$$ .
